solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Man left in class (6)

indicatorNotes.in: 'in' places the left marker inside the word for class, the way a pupil sits in a class

blocks.note: a caste is a rigid social class
L = left, as on a map or stage directions

annotation.surface: A man left behind in a classroom.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Man' is a chess term here: any chess piece is a man, and the castle is the old name for the rook.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: in chess the pieces are called men, and the castle is one of them.

entries.clue: Sock, clothing (7)

blocks.note: as a verb, to sock someone is to punch them hard
British slang for clothes and gear, as in 'get your gear on'

annotation.surface: A list of garments: a sock among the clothing.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sock' sits beside 'clothing' as if it were a garment, but it is the verb to hit; CLOBBER covers both the punch and the British slang for clothes.
annotation.definitionFit: Two unrelated senses of one word: the verb to hit hard, and a British slang noun for one's clothes.

entries.clue: Patience: lose it when upset about broadcast (9)

indicatorNotes.when upset: something upset is knocked over, so its letters no longer stand in order
indicatorNotes.about: 'about' means around, so the rearranged letters wrap round the next piece

blocks.note: anagram fodder, rearranged to split round the middle piece
to air a show is to broadcast it

annotation.surface: Advice to someone whose patience is running out: don't lose your temper over what's on TV.
annotation.walkthrough: Patience is the British name for the one-player card game Americans call solitaire, so the opening word is a game, not a virtue.
annotation.definitionFit: A regional use: British players call the single-player card game patience, Americans call it by the answer.

entries.clue: Cream smeared on it, looking for topping? (6)

indicatorNotes.smeared: smeared letters are spread about and lose their shape
indicatorNotes.for topping: in a down answer a topping sits above the rest, so this piece goes first

blocks.note: lo! is an old call meaning look!, as in 'lo and behold'
anagram fodder, 4 letters

annotation.surface: Someone smearing cream on a dessert and hoping it will pass as a topping.
annotation.walkthrough: The dessert picture makes 'Cream' look like whipped cream, but it is the kind you rub into skin.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the cosmetic sense: a skin cream and this are both emollients you smear on.

entries.clue: Rapidly grow reputation finally in broadcast when leading party (8)

indicatorNotes.finally: 'finally' points at the word's final letter
indicatorNotes.in: 'in' puts that letter inside the word for broadcast
indicatorNotes.when leading: a piece leading another goes in front of it, here ahead of the party

blocks.note: to sow seed broadcast is to scatter it by hand
last letter of reputation
a ball is a formal dancing party

annotation.surface: A politician's reputation grows fast once they are seen on air leading the party.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface makes 'party' political and 'broadcast' about television; one is a dance, the other is sowing seed by scattering.
annotation.definitionFit: A figurative verb: things that grow ever faster are said to do what a rolling ball of snow does, gathering size.

entries.clue: Par for the course in Troon or Muirfield (4)

indicatorNotes.in: 'in' says the answer lies inside the words that follow

blocks.note: the letters run from the end of Troon, through 'or', into the start of Muirfield

annotation.surface: Talk of par on famous Scottish golf courses; Troon and Muirfield both host the Open Championship.
annotation.walkthrough: The golf picture is complete: 'par for the course' reads as golf, but it is the idiom for what is usual.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: whatever is par for the course is the usual standard, what you would expect.

entries.clue: Vital thing, where to go for battle (8)

blocks.note: the thing every living thing needs
loo is British slang for the toilet, where you 'go'

annotation.surface: Directions to somewhere essential before a battle.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Where to go' is a euphemism for the toilet, not a direction.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the 1815 battle where Napoleon was finally defeated.

entries.clue: Pasty Shane chewed up (5)

indicatorNotes.chewed up: food chewed up is mangled out of shape, so the letters are too

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 5 letters

annotation.surface: A man named Shane eating a pasty, the British baked pastry with a filling.
annotation.walkthrough: A pasty is a Cornish pastry, so the surface is about food; the definition is the adjective meaning pale.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a pasty face is pale and unhealthy-looking, grey like ash.

entries.clue: Tory let off, almost no chance of winning? (7)

annotation.definitionNote: a definition by description: the answer is a noun, described by its odds

indicatorNotes.off: something off is not right, so the letters are wrong in order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 7 letters

annotation.surface: A Conservative gets let off, though at the polls they would have almost no chance of winning.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark flags a playful definition: the answer is described only by its famously long odds.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by description: a national draw is known for the tiny chance that any ticket wins.

entries.clue: Boring in empty office in recent years (2,4)

indicatorNotes.in: 'in' puts the first word inside the next
indicatorNotes.empty: an empty word has lost its contents, keeping only its outside letters

blocks.note: office with its middle removed
flat = dull, lifeless

annotation.surface: A complaint that work in a half-empty office has been dull lately.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Boring' looks like drilling or dull work, but it is just the adjective dull; the empty office is its two outside letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym phrase: both mean lately, in the recent past.

entries.clue: Knitter’s heart invested in needlework, note (8)

indicatorNotes.heart: the heart of a word is its middle
indicatorNotes.invested in: money invested in something is put inside it, and so is this letter

blocks.note: crochet is needlework done with a hook
a middle letter of KNITTER

annotation.surface: A knitter pours their heart into their needlework and leaves a note.
annotation.walkthrough: The needlework surface hides music: the answer is the British name for a quarter note.
annotation.definitionFit: A regional use: British musicians call a quarter note by this name.

entries.clue: Vague imprint in blue (7)

indicatorNotes.in: 'in' puts the first piece inside the second

blocks.note: the blue overhead
to etch is to cut a design into a surface

annotation.surface: A faint mark printed in blue ink.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Blue' reads as a colour of ink, but the noun 'the blue' is the sky, as in 'out of the blue'.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: anything drawn only in rough outline lacks detail and is vague.

entries.clue: Too much put on the counter in dollars — for a cheeky couple? (8)

indicatorNotes.put on the counter: counter means contrary, so the letters run against their order
indicatorNotes.in: 'in' puts the turned piece inside the dollars

blocks.note: OTT = over the top, too much
bucks is slang for dollars

annotation.surface: An overcharge at the shop counter, paid in dollars by a cheeky couple.
annotation.walkthrough: The 'cheeky couple' is a pun: a pair of cheeks, the ones you sit on.
annotation.definitionFit: A cryptic pun: the rear has two cheeks, so it is literally a 'cheeky' couple.

entries.clue: Little bit disturbed by new music genre (6)

indicatorNotes.disturbed by: something disturbed by an intruder is broken into, so the letter pushes inside

blocks.note: a trace is a tiny amount
N = new

annotation.surface: Someone slightly unsettled by a new style of music.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Little bit disturbed' reads as a mood, but 'little bit' is the word being broken into.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a style of repetitive electronic dance music named for its hypnotic effect.

entries.clue: Level in corporation, above which skills on the rise (7)

indicatorNotes.above which: in a down answer, 'above which' puts this piece on top of the corporation
indicatorNotes.on the rise: something on the rise goes up, and in a down answer that reads bottom to top

blocks.note: arts = skills, crafts
a corporation is an old jokey word for a pot belly

annotation.surface: Talk of rank in a company, with skills rising above it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Corporation' looks like a business but is old slang for a large belly.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym from geology and sociology: a layer, one level of many.

entries.clue: Bar in Canberra I like (4)

indicatorNotes.in: 'in' says the answer lies inside the words that follow

blocks.note: the letters run from the end of Canberra, through 'I', into 'like'

annotation.surface: An Australian naming a favourite pub in Canberra.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bar' wants to be a pub, but it is a length of metal or wood.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a horizontal bar, as in a towel or hand one.

entries.clue: Frozen assets of writer for the auditor? (10)

indicatorNotes.for the auditor: an auditor is literally a listener, so this is about how a word sounds

blocks.note: a writer's kit: paper, pens, envelopes

annotation.surface: An auditor examining a writer's frozen assets.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Frozen assets' and 'auditor' paint a finance scene; the auditor is simply a hearer, and the two words differ only in one vowel.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: something frozen in place is not moving.

entries.clue: Too much to carry for bird (9)

annotation.definitionNote: the first definition is a phrase for a burden; the answer is a noun

blocks.note: a burden that weighs you down, from the dead seabird hung round the neck in The Rime of the Ancient Mariner
a great ocean seabird

annotation.surface: A load that is too heavy for a bird to lift.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface pictures a bird struggling with a load; the load is the bird itself, the Mariner's millstone.
annotation.definitionFit: Two senses: the huge seabird, and figuratively a burden, after Coleridge's poem.

entries.clue: Canine, one attached to elastic? (8)

blocks.note: a breed of spaniel, so named for springing game from cover
a bungee jumper on elastic bounces up and down

annotation.surface: A dog on an elastic lead.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the playful second half: someone on a bungee cord is one who springs.
annotation.definitionFit: Two senses: a spaniel breed, and jokily anyone who springs, like a bungee jumper.

entries.clue: He’s deeply sorry about a dozy type (10)

indicatorNotes.sorry: something in a sorry state is in a mess, like these letters

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 9 letters
joins the fodder

annotation.surface: A man apologising sincerely for a lazy colleague.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sorry' reads as an apology but means in a poor state, and the apostrophe in 'He's' is dropped.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: an affectionate name for a drowsy person.

entries.clue: Lonely day for old ruler (7)

blocks.note: solo = alone
Mon = Monday

annotation.surface: A lonely day for an ancient king.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Day' can be any of seven abbreviations; the crossing letters pick Monday.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the biblical king of Israel famed for his wisdom.

entries.clue: A stake in back (4)

blocks.note: as written
money staked on an outcome, a wager

annotation.surface: A stake driven into someone's back, vampire style.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Back' reads as a body part but is the verb to support, and 'stake' is a wager, not a post.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to back someone is to support them, usually in wrongdoing here.

entries.clue: Russian author opening up before play (7)

indicatorNotes.up: in a down answer, 'up' means read from the bottom
indicatorNotes.before: 'before' puts this piece ahead of the next

blocks.note: a narrow opening, as for coins
to toy with something is to play with it

annotation.surface: A Russian writer opening up about his play before its premiere.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Opening up' reads as confiding, but it is a noun turned upside down in this down entry.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the Russian novelist who wrote War and Peace.

entries.clue: Grind over surface — tight corner (6)

blocks.note: to rub something hard across a surface
a predicament, a fix you get into

annotation.surface: A car grinding along a wall as it takes a tight corner.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Tight corner' reads as a road bend, but it is a figurative spot of trouble.
annotation.definitionFit: Two senses: the verb for rubbing roughly across, and the noun for an awkward predicament.

entries.clue: Cross-Channel journey, might you say? Really go for it! (3,3)

indicatorNotes.might you say?: 'say' points to how the words are spoken, not spelt

blocks.note: mock French for 'the trip', as a journey across the English Channel into France might be called

annotation.surface: A cheer for someone setting off on a trip to France.
annotation.walkthrough: The Channel is the sea between England and France, so a cross-Channel journey is 'le trip' in Franglais; run together it is the answer.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: to go all out, holding nothing back.

entries.clue: Rule that may also be drawn up? (5)

blocks.clueFragment: that may also be drawn up?
blocks.note: in a down entry, written upward the word reads the same

annotation.surface: A rule for pulling something upward.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Drawn up' sounds like drafting a rule, but it means written bottom to top in this down entry, and the word reads the same both ways.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a principle or rule someone holds to.

entries.clue: Wine came with lust, worryingly (8)

indicatorNotes.worryingly: things going worryingly are going wrong, and so is the order of these letters

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 8 letters; 'with' joins the two words

annotation.surface: Wine arrived and brought desire with it, alarmingly.
annotation.walkthrough: 'With' only glues the two fodder words together and contributes no letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a sweet wine made from muscat grapes.

entries.clue: Top of head shaved in the past (4)

indicatorNotes.Top of: in a down answer the top is the first letter
indicatorNotes.shaved: shaving cuts something off, here that first letter

blocks.note: bonce is British slang for the head
B taken off the top

annotation.surface: Someone whose crown was shaved long ago.
annotation.walkthrough: Bonce is British slang for head; shave off its first letter.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: formerly, at some earlier time.

entries.clue: Fellow, advanced in years, running (8)

blocks.note: a fellow is a man
getting old, American spelling without the E

annotation.surface: An elderly man out jogging.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Running' is not jogging but being in charge.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to run a business is to be in charge of it.

entries.clue: Bizarre portal, perhaps? (3,3)

blocks.note: slang for weird, far out
a door is one example of an exit

annotation.surface: A strange doorway to somewhere else.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark marks 'portal' as one example of an exit, not the only one.
annotation.definitionFit: Two senses: slang for unconventional, and literally an exit, of which a portal is one kind.

entries.clue: On no account sign for legal officials (8)

blocks.note: in no way
a sign of the zodiac, the ram

annotation.surface: A warning never to sign anything for the lawyers.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sign' looks like the verb to put your name down, but it is a star sign.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: officials who witness and certify legal documents.

entries.clue: My sale, awfully awfully small (6)

indicatorNotes.awfully: something done awfully is done badly, so the letters come out wrong

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 6 letters

annotation.surface: A seller lamenting how tiny the takings from their sale were.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Awfully' does two jobs in a row: the first scrambles, the second belongs to the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: contemptibly, disappointingly small.
